title: When to Pay Less and Still Keep the Shelf Space
documentTitle: BC Deal Review: Agenda for Thursday, March 19 — US Carrier RSA Structure
excerptForBlog:
We have one topic scheduled for BC review Thursday: a proposed update to the Revenue Share Agreement (RSA) structure for carriers.

Asks for BC: Approve updated US carrier RSA structure that includes fewer configuration requirements (shift from full search integration to Default Home Screen, or DHS); reduced US carrier revenue share on new devices (no change to installed base); allows exception for Verizon only to allow Yahoo Home mobile app with Bing-powered Yahoo Search bar preloaded on +1 screen (not DHS); and delegation of authority to Platforms & Ecosystems Cross-Functional Deal Review (PEX) to determine how to utilize savings from reduced revenue share. Current plans include volume incentives for premium devices and longer term initiatives to drive Android share.

Rationale in support of deal: Incentive realignment appropriate given current trends whereby US carrier revenue share spend is growing YoY while Android is losing share. Savings from the new RSA structure can self-fund bounties in years 1-2 to drive targeted devices, and be redeployed in year 3+ to help grow the Android ecosystem. Search usage not expected to be materially impacted as long as Google retains placement on DHS. Relaxing configuration requirements to allow preloads of alternative Search apps helps ease regulatory risk and reinforces Google's principle to provide options to users. Carveout for Verizon allows partner to advance their current post-acquisition strategy for distribution of first-party applications across their user base.

lessonTitle: When to Pay Less and Still Keep the Shelf Space
pullQuote: Sometimes the smartest negotiation move is paying your partners less — if you can redirect that money to win the customers who matter most.
leadershipTraits: Fixes broken incentives instead of accepting them
Thinks about regulatory exposure as a deal variable
Distinguishes between what was paid for and what was actually needed
Separates strategic decisions from operational execution
situation: On March 17, 2020, Google's Michael Murphy circulated an agenda memo ahead of a Business Council (BC) review scheduled for March 19. The memo asks senior decision-makers to approve a new deal structure with US mobile carriers. The core tension: Google's carrier revenue-share spending was 'growing YoY while Android is losing share' — money going up, results going down.
insight: The memo reveals a disciplined diagnostic move: when a spend category decouples from outcomes, don't just cut it — redesign where it goes. Google proposes reducing carrier revenue share on new devices, then routing those savings into 'volume incentives for premium devices' in years 1–2 and longer-term Android ecosystem investments in year 3+. The savings self-fund the next lever rather than disappearing into margin. This is classic reinvestment logic inside a distribution deal, not a blanket cost reduction. There's a second move embedded here. The memo frames relaxing configuration requirements — allowing rival search apps to be preloaded — as simultaneously easing 'regulatory risk' and reinforcing user choice. The Verizon carve-out (permitting a Yahoo/Bing-powered search bar on a secondary screen, not the default home screen) handles a specific partner need without surrendering the default placement that the memo identifies as the real driver: 'Search usage not expected to be materially impacted as long as Google retains placement on DHS.'
application: Audit any recurring partnership spend where costs are rising but your key metric (share, retention, revenue) is flat or declining. Before cutting, map where the freed dollars could create better leverage — a volume incentive, a product investment, a stickier integration. Then negotiate an exit from the old structure that gives the partner something real (like the Verizon carve-out) so the relationship survives the change.
